answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: In an integrated national REC market where REC buyers are responsive to REC prices (like the US voluntary market), the supply response and therefore emissions impact will be determined in the aggregate, not by the details of individual procurement details. As a result, it is inaccurate to think of different marginal emissions impacts for each procurement during a period of time. Any new procurement Q will add to aggregate demand that will raise REC prices nationally and stimulate new renewable projects on the aggregate supply curve. Therefore, all the procurements should receive the same marginal emissions impact during the year, equal to the average marginal impact of all the procurement.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
The complete long-term emissions impact of the procurement should be considered at the time of the procurement. The impacts include:
1. The immediate price impacts: higher spot and futures prices for REC's, lower spot and futures prices in electricity markets where new generation is likely to be built, higher variance in electricity prices
2. The long-term change in generation mix and emissions: in response to the change in prices, new renewable generation comes on line, storage/DR/transmission capacity increases, new fossil fuel plants are delayed and/or existing fossil fuel plants are retired, and emissions are permanently lowered from the alternative baseline.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: There should be a common marginal emissions impact for all procurement each year. The marginal emissions impact wouldn't change much each year, reflecting gradual changes in the mix of coal vs natural gas impacts.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: The REC market, like other markets, is inherently additional and does not require separate additionality tests. Every procurement increases aggregate demand which raises prices to a market-clearing level that stimulates a matching quantity of new supply. Some have assumed that REC markets stop working because of "oversupply", disrupting "additionality". But this assumption is not supported by the market evidence (all REC's sold at positive prices) and inconsistent with standard economic assumptions (i.e.; that buyers and sellers respond to prices, which causes markets to find an equilibrium and clear).

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: There could be one market-wide test to check that the market is in fact clearing normally: Do suppliers tend to sell their REC's at a positive price?

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: Not if voluntary REC buyers are allowed to respond dynamically to low-priced REC's in different regions, which would ensure sufficient demand and positive REC prices in all regions.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: Marginal emission impacts should be calculated at the aggregate level and used for all procurement during the year.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: With an integrated US-wide REC market, aggregate marginal emissions rates should be applied to all procurement during the year. Similarly for an integrated EU-wide market, aggregate emissions rates should be applied to all EU procurement during the year.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Aggregate emissions rates for all procurement during a year, recalculated annually.
